issues.what: The key restates the stem's own premise. The pores 'hold back bacteria' and the cause 'came through', so 'It was smaller than bacteria' follows from the stem's words with no virology. It is also the T2 fact (the-microscope-and-cell-theory keys viruses as too small for a light microscope). All that is left is to decline the over-readings, and a test-wise player simply takes the most cautious claim, which is also the shortest choice (28 characters against 32-38).
issues.fix: Make a cautious-sounding over-reading compete. Key: 'It was smaller than the bacteria the filter caught'. Replace 'It was a new kind of living germ' with 'It could not be a bacterium of any kind'. Ivanovsky himself thought it might be an extremely small bacterium (F9), so the filter alone could not rule that out. Keep 'a poison that bacteria made' and 'could multiply inside living leaves'.

issues.what: 'Repeated the filter test' assumes the player has just seen the Ivanovsky question. Questions are drawn one at a time, so the filter test may be unknown to him.
issues.fix: 'Martinus Beijerinck passed sap from tobacco plants with mosaic disease, which mottles the leaves, through a filter that holds back bacteria in 1898, and the sap still made plants sick. Then he infected a healthy plant...'

issues.what: 'It is a single cell, but with no nucleus' is dead as a reason for counting a thing not alive. By cell theory a single cell is alive (cells-the-building-blocks-of-life, T2, keys a bacterium as 'one whole living cell'), so the choice argues against itself. Only two lures are live.
issues.fix: Replace it with 'It is far too small to count as a living thing'. This is the size misconception that the unit's own filter story invites.

issues.what: The stem says 'in 1935'. facts.md F12 says the stem avoids leaning on the year, because a Hamburg page dates true crystals to 1937.
issues.fix: Say 'in the 1930s', or have the fact-checker confirm 1935 for the needle-shaped crystals.

issues.what: 'Needle-shaped crystals, as a pure chemical forms' reads awkwardly.
issues.fix: '...into fine, needle-shaped crystals, like those of a pure chemical.'

issues.what: The stem names the variable ('whether the killing needed the living mould itself'), and the key is the only choice that takes the living mould away. The player answers by matching the stem. 'Look at the dead bacteria under a far stronger microscope' tempts no one, and 'Grow the mould alone on a fresh dish with no bacteria' tests nothing about killing, so neither is a mistake a 9th grader really makes when designing a test.
issues.fix: Keep the key and 'Set the mould on a dish of a different kind of bacteria'. Replace the microscope choice with 'Repeat the same dish many times with fresh mould', the classic confusion of repeating with isolating. Replace 'Grow the mould alone...' with 'Grow the mould and the bacteria on the dish for longer'. Both look like careful science but leave the mould and the killing together.

issues.what: 'It killed only bacteria that cause no disease' is weak. The stem calls the substance bacteria-killing, and every player knows penicillin went on to cure infections.
issues.fix: Replace it with 'A patent kept other laboratories from making it'. That is false, since Fleming took out no patent, but it must first be sourced in facts.md. Otherwise use 'Fleming would not share his mould with other laboratories', which is also false and also needs a source.

issues.what: Two lures are dead. 'That it could kill streptococci in a dish' is plainly not what a test on living mice shows. 'That no kind of bacteria could ever resist it' is an overclaim that no single experiment could show. Only 'That it did an animal no harm when injected' competes with the key.
issues.fix: Replace the two with 'That it would cure sick people as it cured mice' and 'That enough of it could be made to treat a person'. The Oxford team still had to test the first, and the Albert Alexander case (F24) shows the second was not yet true. Both are honest over-readings of a mouse result.

issues.what: The stem's clauses eliminate the lures. 'Not close relatives' and 'within a few years' rule out 'Both kinds inherited it from a shared ancestor'. The planted sentence 'New mutations that give resistance are rare, at most about one cell in a million' rules out 'Each kind hit on the very same mutation by chance'. 'The antibiotic changed both kinds' genes the same way' is the misconception T3 natural-and-artificial-selection already keys as wrong (its flies' 'The spray changed the flies' genes'). So the key is left by elimination, and no knowledge that bacteria share genes is needed.
issues.fix: Cut the mutation-rate sentence. Make the tempting lure the T3 idea itself, so that the question goes a grade deeper. Stem: 'Doctors at a hospital find the very same gene for resisting one antibiotic, base for base, in two kinds of bacteria that are not close relatives. It has spread through both kinds within a few years. How did it most likely reach both?' Choices: 'Bacteria passed copies of it directly to one another' / 'Each kind evolved it as its resistant cells multiplied' / 'The antibiotic changed both kinds' genes the same way' / 'Both kinds inherited it from a shared ancestor'. Only the gene being the very same, base for base, in unrelated kinds separates sharing from separate selection.

issues.what: T3 natural-and-artificial-selection uses 'Resistant flies passed it on to others by touch' as a WRONG choice. This key says that bacteria do pass resistance directly. A player who met both may think the units contradict each other.
issues.fix: Add to the card: 'Animals cannot hand genes to one another, but bacteria can, even to bacteria of another kind.'

issues.what: This re-asks T3 natural-and-artificial-selection. Its chest-infection question keys 'The bacteria, as resistant ones lived and multiplied', against the lures 'Her body, as it grew used to the drug' and 'each one learned to stand the drug'. Its flies question has 'The spray changed the flies' genes'. Here the key 'They favour resistance genes that already exist' is that same fact, and two of the lures, 'make bacteria build new genes' and 'make the patient's own body resist them', are T3's lures again. The ancient permafrost is new evidence, but the fact keyed is not. The stem's 'long before anyone made a medicine' also all but states the key.
issues.fix: Re-key on what the find adds (F29): where such genes came from. Keep the stem up to 'vancomycin among them', then ask: 'Why did bacteria carry such genes so long before any medicine?' Key: 'Soil microbes have long made antibiotics against one another'. Lures: 'Bacteria build every gene they might one day need' (the forward-planning misconception), 'The ice-age cold made their genes change faster' and 'Mammoths carried them into the ground from other lands'. The writer may find a better fourth. The card keeps 'a drug writes no resistance genes' as background, not as the key.

unit_notes: Overlaps. fc2f10c230 re-asks T3 natural-and-artificial-selection (high, re-key given). f980be0ae6's gene sharing is new ground, but as written it is solved by elimination. 4d8eeceb5c's key fact (a virus is smaller than a bacterium) is T2 ground (the-microscope-and-cell-theory keys the electron microscope's viruses; cells-the-building-blocks-of-life uses 'A kind of virus, not a cell' as a lure). Only its 'on its own' reasoning lifts it to T5, hence the fix. e94c2cdda1 does not re-ask the-bodys-defences: that unit keys that colds come from many viruses, this one why antibiotics cannot touch them. 8f9cef4c25 does not re-ask the T2 'a bacterium is one living cell'. Nothing touches how-germs-were-proven's Pasteur or Koch. Its Koch card mentions that viruses cannot be grown outside living cells, which 8f9cef4c25 keys, but a card line is not a keyed question, so this is fine. Within the batch, from-dna-to-protein's Hershey-Chase stem calls a phage 'DNA in a protein coat', which fits this unit's card on what a virus is. Safety is clean: no enhancement, engineering, culturing method, transmissibility or virulence detail, and no vaccines. The gene sharing in f980be0ae6 stays at textbook level (plasmids are named only in the card). Beijerinck's 'would grow in no broth, only in living tissue' is the definition of a virus, not a method. Shape: three tobacco-mosaic and three penicillin questions. The scope is covered (a virus not counted alive, its size, antibiotics against bacteria not viruses, Fleming's dish of 1928, resistance). With fc2f10c230 re-keyed, resistance still has two questions on ground new to T5. d0b1168be3 and 0a3e5014e4 both draw on F20 (Fleming found it harmless), but only as lures and context, so they are different facts.
